client: I've been really stressed out lately because I got a lower grade than I expected on my last exam, and now I'm terrified it's going to tank my GPA. I keep running the numbers over and over in my head, trying to figure out if I can still pull off a perfect score, and it's just exhausting. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grade is already there and nothing can undo it.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now — the stress of the grade itself, plus this exhausting mental loop of trying to calculate your way out of the anxiety. I also notice you mentioned some doubt about whether talking will even help, and I want to gently sit with that for a moment — sometimes that feeling of "nothing can change it" is actually part of what makes the stress feel so stuck. What do you think it would mean for you *beyond* the GPA if this grade stayed as it is?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess if the grade just... stayed, it would mean I actually failed at something I told myself I'd be good at. Like, I've always been the person who figures it out, who pulls through, and this feels like proof that maybe I'm not that person anymore. It's hard to even say that out loud because it sounds so dramatic, but it's like the grade is evidence of something worse than just a bad semester.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage — that this grade feels like evidence against a story you've built your identity around, "I'm someone who figures it out." That's such a painful place to be, and it makes complete sense that it feels bigger than just a semester. I'm curious — when you say you're "not that person anymore," is there a part of you that believes one grade actually has the power to rewrite everything you've already proven about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically I know one grade shouldn't define everything. But in the moment, it really does feel like it cancels out all the times I did figure it out, like those don't count anymore. And yeah, I guess part of me does believe it has that power, which is terrifying to even admit out loud.
therapist: The fact that you can name that — "part of me believes it has that power" — is actually a really important moment, because it means you're starting to see it as a *belief* rather than a *fact*. In CBT, we'd call what's happening an "all-or-nothing" pattern, where one piece of contradicting evidence feels like it wipes the whole slate clean — but that's the anxiety talking, not reality. What do you think it would take for one of those past "I figured it out" moments to actually count again in your mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess it does feel a little different to think of it as a belief instead of just... the truth. But honestly, even if I can name it that way right now, in the moment when the anxiety hits, it doesn't feel like a belief at all — it feels completely real and certain. I think what it would take for those past moments to count is if I could somehow hold onto them when things get hard, but that's exactly when they disappear on me.
therapist: You've just identified something really precise and important — it's not that you *don't know* these past moments exist, it's that anxiety acts like a thief that steals your access to them exactly when you need them most. What we can work on together is building what I'd call an "anchor" — a way to make those memories more retrievable under pressure, so they're not so easily swept away. Would you be open to exploring what one of those "I figured it out" moments felt like, so we can start making it more vivid and easier to hold onto?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess that makes sense, the "thief" thing... it does feel like that sometimes, like the good memories just vanish when I'm panicking. But I'm a little skeptical about whether focusing on one old memory is really going to help in the moment when everything feels like it's falling apart. I mean, I can try to think of something, but I'm already worried it won't feel real enough to actually calm me down when the anxiety hits.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and I actually think it's worth trusting — because you're right that just *thinking* of a memory won't automatically calm a panic response. What we'd really be aiming for is less about recalling a fact and more about practicing accessing that feeling of capability *before* the crisis hits, so it becomes a well-worn path rather than a locked door. Would it feel more believable if we thought of it less as a magic fix and more as a small experiment — something low-stakes to try and see what actually happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess "small experiment" makes it sound less like I have to commit to something that might fail. But honestly, I'm still not sure when I'd even practice it — my days feel so chaotic and full of dread already that adding one more thing feels like pressure, not relief. Like, what if I try it and it just doesn't work, and then I feel even more hopeless than before?
therapist: The fear that trying and failing would feel worse than not trying at all — that's such a honest and important thing to name, and it tells me the stakes feel really high right now even around small things. I want to gently turn that thought over with you: what does it say about where you are that even a low-pressure experiment feels like it could confirm something terrible about yourself? That might actually be the most important thing for us to look at together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... yeah, that hits something. Like, even thinking about reaching out to someone, just texting a friend I haven't talked to in a while, feels like I'm setting myself up to find out that they don't actually care, or that I've been forgotten. And if that happens, it's not just about the text anymore, it kind of confirms this thing I already half-believe, that I'm not worth keeping around.
therapist: What you just said is really significant — this isn't just about a grade or a text anymore, it's touching something much deeper, this fear that you might not be worth keeping around. I want to make sure I'm sitting with that carefully, because that's a painful belief to be carrying, and I imagine it's been there longer than this semester. Can I ask — when do you think you first started half-believing that about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know, it's hard to pinpoint exactly... but I think it started pretty young, maybe middle school or so, when my friend group kind of just quietly stopped including me in things. Like, there was no big fight or anything, I just slowly noticed I wasn't being invited anymore, and I never really understood why, and I think that's almost worse because I filled in the blank myself with "it must be something wrong with me."
therapist: That quiet kind of exclusion can be so much harder to heal than an open conflict, because your mind had to write the ending itself — and it wrote the cruelest version. The story "it must be something wrong with me" made sense to a younger you trying to explain something painful and confusing, but it was a child's best guess, not the truth. I'm wondering, if you could go back and offer that younger version of yourself another possible explanation for what happened, what might it be?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I sit with that for a moment, because it's not a question I've ever really let myself ask. I think... maybe the other explanation is that those kids were just caught up in their own worlds, their own little groups, and I happened to be on the outside of something that wasn't really about me at all. But honestly, even saying that out loud, part of me doesn't fully believe it — like my gut still insists there had to be a reason, and that reason had to be me.
therapist: You just did something really brave — you generated a kinder explanation, even if your gut isn't fully on board with it yet, and that gap between what your mind can reason and what your body still believes is exactly where this old wound lives. It makes sense that the gut feeling is stubborn; it's had decades of practice, while the new explanation is only a few seconds old. What do you notice happening inside you right now, even just physically, as you sit with both of those explanations at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I notice my chest feels kind of tight, like there's this pressure sitting right in the middle of it. And my shoulders are up near my ears, which I didn't even realize until you asked. It's strange because my head can kind of hold both explanations at the same time, but my body is clearly voting hard for the old one.
therapist: Your body is being such an honest witness right now — that tightness and those raised shoulders are the old story holding on, doing what it's always done to keep you braced for rejection. What's really meaningful is that you noticed it, because that moment of noticing is actually a tiny crack of distance between you and the belief, proof that you're not completely fused with it. Can you try, just for a moment, to take one slow breath and see if your shoulders are willing to drop even slightly — not to fix anything, just to see what happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
